newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Yeltsin set for heart tests, PM to visit Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Yeltsin set for heart tests, PM to visit Chechnya.

text.p: Doctors have cancelled all Russian President Boris Yeltsin's meetings for the next week to carry out routine tests in the last stage of preparations for his heart surgery, a Kremlin spokesman said on Monday.
"Planned preparations for the heart surgery have entered the final stage," presidential spokesman Sergei Yastrzhembsky told a news briefing in the Kremlin.

Despite Yeltsin's absence, efforts to tackle political problems continued. His Chechnya envoy said Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin was likely to make an unprecedented visit to the rebel region soon in efforts to help peace moves.

The Kremlin also announced that Yeltsin had started procedures to remove former bodyguard and confidant Alexander Korzhakov from the military, a move which appeared designed to step up the president's drive to end political intrigues.

Yastrzhembsky said Yeltsin's tests had been planned in advance and played down their significance. He did not say when the operation, to improve the blood supply to Yeltsin's heart, would take place but said it would not be this week.

"The president will undergo a whole series of medical tests under a special regime in the next few days," he said. "That is why, following the recommendation of the council of doctors, all his meetings for the next week have been cancelled."
Yeltsin, 65, has been holding brief but regular meetings in the past few weeks at the sanatorium outside Moscow where he is preparing for his operation.
The Kremlin has repeatedly dismissed rumours that Yeltsin's health is worse than doctors say, and it insists the operation will go ahead in the second half of November.

While Yeltsin prepares for surgery, Chernomyrdin has taken on some of his duties. Yeltsin's envoy to Chechnya, Ivan Rybkin, said Chernomyrdin was expected to visit Chechnya "in the near future" for peace talks.
"The prime minister's participation in the negotiation process and in solving a whole series of urgent problems is becoming indispensible," Rybkin told Ekho Moskvy radio station.
It would be Chernomyrdin's first known visit to Chechnya since Moscow sent troops to the southern region to try to crush its independence drive in December 1994.

Chechnya, where peace remains fragile despite a nearly three-month-old ceasefire, is one of the main problems Yeltsin faces. A solution to the question of its political status, in or out of Russia, remains distant.
NTV commercial television broadcast an interview with Chernomyrdin on Monday which allowed a rare glimpse of the prime minister's family and personal life.

Chernomyrdin, 58, was seen at his state dacha, or weekend home, sipping tea with his grandson on his knee and chatting with his wife. NTV showed him playing a tune on the piano accordion, sitting chatting by a bonfire and playing billiards.

Chernomyrdin has kept a backseat while others around him jostle for position in Yeltsin's absence. He has not announced any presidential ambitions but looked every bit a potential presidential candidate in Monday's television interview.
Yeltsin has been trying hard to stamp out the manouevring for position by other senior officials.
In a move designed to show he is ready to get tough to end the squabbling, the Kremlin confirmed on Monday that Yeltsin had issued an order on Sunday to oust Korzhakov from the military.

Korzhakov's disgrace was a punishment for criticising the president's entourage and threatening to reveal dark secrets about the Kremlin following his dismissal as Yeltsin's bodyguard in June. It will have little effect on the balance of power.
But the humiliation of a man who until recently had immense influence was a clear signal that Yeltsin demands total loyalty.
